power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Although notions of a 'winning mindset' are repeatedly put forth in self-help books, podcasts, and sport psychology publications, there appears to be little to no compelling evidence that such a mindset exists.
The aim of the current study was to investigate the beliefs elite athletes hold about the nature of winning and to examine whether these beliefs may suggest a winning mindset.
Using a theoryinformed qualitative design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with nine athletes who had represented New Zealand across seven sports.
Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis with a hybrid inductive-deductive approach.
Results suggest that athletes conceptualise winning in two markedly different ways.
Winning-is-Proving comprises beliefs that winning means beating others and not losing, whereas Winning-is-Improving comprises beliefs that winning means self-betterment and realising one's potential.
These beliefs were associated with coherent patterns of goals, expectations, and attributions, providing support for their interpretation as a mindset about winning.

To our knowledge, these results provide the first preliminary evidence for the existence of a winning mindset and, in doing so, lay the groundwork for research currently underway to develop and validate winning mindset as a novel psychological construct.
Implications for mindset theory and sport psychology, as well as for coaches and support staff working with elite athletes, are considered.
One of the most common pieces of advice that elite athletes receive is to 'have a winning mindset'.
Over the years, an abundance of books, articles, and commentary have disseminated this rhetoric (e.g., Brat et al., 2025; Hughes, 2016; Niethe, 2024; Seversen, 2021).
text.formatted: Over the years, an abundance of books, articles, and commentary have disseminated this rhetoric (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Brat et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Hughes, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Niethe, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Seversen, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, despite its widespread use, there is little to no convincing evidence that a distinct winning mindset exists in athletes or other populations.
Moreover, little is known about the beliefs athletes hold regarding the nature of winning itself.
Mindsets are core beliefs that people hold about a domain, topic, or category (Zion et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Mindsets are core beliefs that people hold about a domain, topic, or category <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Zion et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Although the terms mindset and belief are often used interchangeably, mindsets are a particular class of beliefs that have motivational value and orient people to specific sets of expectations, attributions, and goals (Dweck, 2019).
text.formatted: Although the terms mindset and belief are often used interchangeably, mindsets are a particular class of beliefs that have motivational value and orient people to specific sets of expectations, attributions, and goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Dweck, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In essence, mindsets help people organise and simplify complex information in ways that produce meaning (e.g., Why is this happening?), create predictions (e.g., What will happen next?), and drive action (e.g., What should I do next?).
As such, their effects are not inconsequential, and mindsets can shape how people feel and act, with consequences for health, wellbeing, and performance (Crum & Zuckerman, 2017).
text.formatted: As such, their effects are not inconsequential, and mindsets can shape how people feel and act, with consequences for health, wellbeing, and performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Crum & Zuckerman, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Mindsets have been extensively studied across a wide range of domains, from intelligence and personality (Dweck & Yeager, 2019) to stress (Crum et al., 2013), exercise (Zahrt & Crum, 2020), and even success (Allan & Rong, 2026).
text.formatted: Mindsets have been extensively studied across a wide range of domains, from intelligence and personality <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Dweck & Yeager, 2019)</ref> to stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Crum et al., 2013)</ref>, exercise <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Zahrt & Crum, 2020)</ref>, and even success <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Allan & Rong, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In the context of sport, research has focused primarily on growth and stress mindsets (McNeil et al., 2024; Spray & Warburton, 2025).
text.formatted: In the context of sport, research has focused primarily on growth and stress mindsets <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(McNeil et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Spray & Warburton, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Growth mindsets have been associated with greater performance and more constructive responses to success and failure (Gontijo et al., 2023; Shaffer et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Growth mindsets have been associated with greater performance and more constructive responses to success and failure <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gontijo et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Shaffer et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, stress-is-enhancing mindsets have been associated with more adaptive coping, greater psychological wellbeing, and lower burnout (Mansell & Turner, 2023; Shipherd et al., 2024), with intervention studies also reporting improvements in perceived performance and psychological functioning (Mansell et al., 2024; Mansell et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Similarly, stress-is-enhancing mindsets have been associated with more adaptive coping, greater psychological wellbeing, and lower burnout <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Mansell & Turner, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Shipherd et al., 2024)</ref>, with intervention studies also reporting improvements in perceived performance and psychological functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Mansell et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Mansell et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Although existing research on growth and stress mindsets in sport provides helpful insights, it does not address athletes' beliefs about the nature and meaning of winning itself.

This distinction is important because an athlete may believe that ability is not fixed or that stress can be beneficial while holding quite different beliefs about winning, which could conceivably evoke changes in emotion, attention, motivation, and outcomes (Walton & Wilson, 2018).
text.formatted: This distinction is important because an athlete may believe that ability is not fixed or that stress can be beneficial while holding quite different beliefs about winning, which could conceivably evoke changes in emotion, attention, motivation, and outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Walton & Wilson, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Recent evidence suggests that the growing popularity of mindset as a concept has led to concerns about oversimplification, confusion, and inconsistent use, prompting calls for greater conceptual clarity and consistency in how mindsets are defined (see Gasteiger & Crum, 2025).
text.formatted: Recent evidence suggests that the growing popularity of mindset as a concept has led to concerns about oversimplification, confusion, and inconsistent use, prompting calls for greater conceptual clarity and consistency in how mindsets are defined (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Gasteiger & Crum, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These concerns are particularly relevant to the winning mindset, for which there is neither an agreed-upon definition nor clear and compelling empirical support.

More specifically, winning mindset appears to be conflated with a variety of established concepts, such as emotional intelligence, self-talk and visualisation (Nicholls, 2021), self-confidence (Lee & Hwang, 2025; Mansell, 2021), mental preparedness (Cabanda, 2021), and mental toughness (Sheard, 2012), to name a few.
text.formatted: More specifically, winning mindset appears to be conflated with a variety of established concepts, such as emotional intelligence, self-talk and visualisation <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Nicholls, 2021)</ref>, self-confidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Lee & Hwang, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Mansell, 2021)</ref>, mental preparedness <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cabanda, 2021)</ref>, and mental toughness <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Sheard, 2012)</ref>, to name a few.

text.text: To further confuse the issue, several publications define winning mindset as an assortment of traits and behaviours (e.g., Beswick, 2015).
text.formatted: To further confuse the issue, several publications define winning mindset as an assortment of traits and behaviours (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Beswick, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: For example, Niethe (2024) describes a winning mindset as comprising fearlessness, the ability to endure criticism, and a strong self-image.

This description is similar in formulation to that of Bolckmans et al. (2023), who define winning mindset as an assemblage of effort, discipline, will to win, motivation, dedication to sport, and perseverance.
text.formatted: This description is similar in formulation to that of <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bolckmans et al. (2023)</ref>, who define winning mindset as an assemblage of effort, discipline, will to win, motivation, dedication to sport, and perseverance.

text.text: Such definitions, while potentially inspiring, ignore the well-established body of research on mindsets (Gasteiger & Crum, 2025).
text.formatted: Such definitions, while potentially inspiring, ignore the well-established body of research on mindsets <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Gasteiger & Crum, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, these inconsistencies are both scientifically and practically problematic.
Without alignment of terminology, winning mindset cannot be reliably distinguished from existing constructs or appropriately operationalised.
Furthermore, it is difficult to establish shared practices or cohesive discourse, while claims that athletes should possess or develop a winning mindset remain unsubstantiated.

As a first step towards addressing these issues, the present research aimed to explore, in detail, the beliefs elite athletes hold about winning and to examine whether these beliefs orient their expectations, attributions, and goals, thereby suggesting a winning mindset.
The study was guided by the following two research questions: RQ1: What beliefs do elite athletes hold about winning?
RQ2: How do these beliefs orient athletes' expectations, attributions, and goals, and does this suggest a winning mindset?
To address the research questions, a theory-informed qualitative design, underpinned by a critical realist ontology and an interpretivist epistemology, was selected (Sparkes & Smith, 2013).
text.formatted: To address the research questions, a theory-informed qualitative design, underpinned by a critical realist ontology and an interpretivist epistemology, was selected <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Sparkes & Smith, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: A critical realist ontology assumes that reality exists independently of human perceptions, while recognising that knowledge of reality is inevitably mediated by social structures, values, and sociocultural contexts (Braun & Clarke, 2021a).
text.formatted: A critical realist ontology assumes that reality exists independently of human perceptions, while recognising that knowledge of reality is inevitably mediated by social structures, values, and sociocultural contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Braun & Clarke, 2021a)</ref>.

text.text: Critical realism further posits a stratified reality in which individuals' experiences and interpretations provide partial access to underlying processes that may help explain them (Bhaskar, 2013).
text.formatted: Critical realism further posits a stratified reality in which individuals' experiences and interpretations provide partial access to underlying processes that may help explain them <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bhaskar, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: An interpretivist epistemology complements this position by asserting that knowledge is situated, partial, and shaped by the meanings individuals assign to their experiences (Atkinson, 2011).
text.formatted: An interpretivist epistemology complements this position by asserting that knowledge is situated, partial, and shaped by the meanings individuals assign to their experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Atkinson, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these commitments call for an approach that is interpretive, context-sensitive, and reflexive.

Correspondingly, semistructured interviews were selected for their suitability in exploring athletes' beliefs about winning while providing flexibility to probe participants' responses in depth (Kallio et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Correspondingly, semistructured interviews were selected for their suitability in exploring athletes' beliefs about winning while providing flexibility to probe participants' responses in depth <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Kallio et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Kim et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Data were analysed using Braun and Clarke's (2022) reflexive thematic analysis with a hybrid inductive-deductive approach.

This aligned with interpretivism by recognising the researcher's active role in interpreting participants' comments and interview responses, and with critical realism by treating those accounts as necessarily partial accounts of athletes' beliefs about winning and how those beliefs function.

In addition, the hybrid approach allowed for the incorporation of the theoretical framework described below while affording the flexibility to interpret participants' responses inductively (Swain, 2018).
text.formatted: In addition, the hybrid approach allowed for the incorporation of the theoretical framework described below while affording the flexibility to interpret participants' responses inductively <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Swain, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The Meaning System component of the generic mindset framework developed by the Stanford Mind & Body Lab (Figure 1) provided the theoretical basis for this investigation.
text.formatted: The Meaning System component of the generic mindset framework developed by the Stanford Mind & Body Lab (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>) provided the theoretical basis for this investigation.

text.text: This framework 'can be applied to a wide-variety of different mindsets'
The research team was composed of two researchers with experience in sport and psychological research.
The lead author had expertise in mindset science and peakperformance psychology, while the second author, an Honours researcher and lifelong athlete, conducted the interviews.
The researchers therefore occupied different 'insider' and 'outsider' positions (Guba & Lincoln, 1994; Pezalla et al., 2012).
text.formatted: The researchers therefore occupied different 'insider' and 'outsider' positions <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Guba & Lincoln, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Pezalla et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, the team's positionality enabled reflexive practice through ongoing discussion, critical examination of assumptions, and consideration of alternative interpretations throughout the analytic process.
This study was reviewed and approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee of the University of Canterbury (Ref: HREC 2023/05/BL).
Athletes were recruited through purposive sampling from professional networks and via snowball sampling.
Elite athletes were defined as those who had represented New Zealand in international competition (adapted from Elwood et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Elite athletes were defined as those who had represented New Zealand in international competition (adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Elwood et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Eligible participants were thus current or retired athletes aged 18 years or older who met this definition.
Data were collected from N = 9 athletes.
The sample comprised six female and three male athletes, with one participant from rowing, running, rugby, motocross, and triathlon, and two from netball and cycling.
Pseudonyms are used in the results to protect participant anonymity.
Prior to taking part, participants received detailed study information and provided written informed consent.
Each participant completed a single online, audio-recorded interview via Microsoft Teams™, lasting 45-65 minutes, and received a $20 supermarket voucher as a token of appreciation.
Consistent with the study's critical realist and interpretivist positioning, the Verbatim transcripts were produced for each interview and returned to participants for review.
No participants requested changes or withdrew after completing an interview.
In keeping with reflexive thematic analysis, data adequacy was judged by the richness of the dataset and its capacity to address the research questions (Braun & Clarke, 2021b).
text.formatted: In keeping with reflexive thematic analysis, data adequacy was judged by the richness of the dataset and its capacity to address the research questions <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Braun & Clarke, 2021b)</ref>.

text.text: Three pretest interviews were conducted before the main interviews to assess the clarity, relevance, and sequencing of the questions.
Minor refinements were subsequently made to the interview guide, and the pretest data were excluded from the analysis.
Trustworthiness was supported through transparency and reflexivity throughout the research process.

text.text: Throughout the interviews, athletes articulated different beliefs about the nature of winning and what it meant within their lives.
We first present four beliefs about winning: realising potential, not losing, self-betterment, and beating others.
We then examine how these beliefs were reflected in athletes' goals, expectations, and attributions, before considering whether these findings are indicative of a mindset about winning.
For some athletes, winning was about realising one's potential.

For those who articulated this belief, winning meant expressing their abilities, talents, and capabilities as fully as possible: We used to just try to win everything . . . and it sort of becomes more motivation to do more, and then it sort of becomes a cycle.
Later on down the track . . . it's just a relief, I guess, sometimes, to not lose.

For other athletes like Isabella, the belief that winning is not losing appeared to influence her performance, such that her focus shifted from her own game towards preventing others from winning: In this respect, winning meant maintaining one's position at the top and preventing others from winning, rather than necessarily improving one's own performance.
Many of the athletes interviewed expressed a belief that winning is self-betterment.
Those who communicated this belief saw winning as becoming better over time.
Here, improvement itself could constitute winning.
For instance, Amelia expressed this belief as follows: 'I think [winning] is very much always bettering myself, whether it's athletically or academically or things like that.'
Amelia went on to say that 'I feel like it's a never-ending cycle where you're bettering yourself and then you just keep moving the goal posts.'
A similar view of winning was given by Zoe, who said: '[Winning] is achieving growth, I think.
So you want to get the growth, and that is the win in itself, experiencing the growth and just, yeah, getting better with everything you do.
Don't want to go backwards.'
Winning, in this sense, means becoming better, with the experience of growth itself representing a win.
Several athletes articulated a belief that winning meant beating others and coming out ahead of the competition.
For example, Liam said: 'It [winning] means you're the best.
You just want to win, you just want to see your name on the trophy and get the prizes.
I used to race and beat people so I could get the win.'

Similarly, Isabella stated that winning meant coming out ahead of others: 'If I'm honest, I think winning is coming out ahead of others, whether that's, um, finishing first or placing . . . in the sense [that], for you to win, other people have to have lost.'

text.text: In this respect, winning was defined by defeating others: to win was to come out ahead of someone else, such that someone else had necessarily lost.
Several recurring facets of beliefs about winning were evident across athletes.

Winning was consistently described as positive and desirable; winning extended beyond sport into other areas of life; and, for some athletes, their beliefs about winning changed over the course of their careers.
One thing stressed by all athletes was that winning itself was inherently positive and desirable.
Athletes consistently described winning as a positive, valued experience that should be pursued.
When asked if she had ever experienced negative or unexpected consequences as a result of winning, Isabella said: 'No . . . not at all . . .
I think winning has, in my history, been a pretty, yeah, positive experience.'
A similar response was expressed by Zoe, who described winning as 'globally positive.'
Sophia described it as 'really cool.
I still think the feeling that you get from winning is the same as what you got when you were a kid.
I still have a desire to win in what I'm doing.'
This belief was also described by Steve, who said that 'For me personally, I see it [winning] as inherently positive.
I think winning reinforces all the good things about sport.'
Likewise, Amelia stated that '[Winning] is something I always strive for, and I don't think it should be avoided.'
Many athletes emphasised that their beliefs about winning went beyond sport, suggesting that their beliefs about winning were not confined to sport but extended into other areas of life.
For example, Steve felt that his view of winning was the same outside of his sport: 'I guess that yeah it applies completely across work and sport.
So whether it be winning a game or completing a project, I think that winning is the same.'
Likewise, Zoe explained that her notion of winning extended to her career: I think from a young age I've always wanted to win, so it's kind of been a wanting aspect in everything I do as well.
Could I keep being better at that?
Whether that be my desk job, I kind of want to be the best at what I do in that aspect, but also in high performance sport.

Going further, Isabella highlighted how winning was an organising principle in her life: I think about it not just as a competition or something, but it can also be just winning in, I'd say, winning in life.
Winning in life always orientates me . . .
I have goals and right across all the types of things you do, career, personal life, acquisition, yeah, all of the financial things, all of that type of thing.
It's how I think about winning is the same.
Several athletes explained how their beliefs about winning shifted over their careers.
Importantly, these shifts in beliefs were described as fundamental changes in how winning was conceptualised, pursued, and evaluated.
When asked if her beliefs about winning had changed over the course of her career, Chloe said: I definitely [did] not always believe that winning was about achieving my potential.
I think when I was [in sport] in school, I felt like I had to win.

In terms, like, I wanted to be the best and then, I had a [sport] partner who kind of made the point that doing your best is the best that you can do anyway, and so then I kind of shifted my mindset to like, I actually just want to enjoy this and do my best.
And whatever that result is, will be.
So I definitely shifted from winning to be better than others to if I win, then that's a result of the hard work I've put in, but it doesn't matter.
A shift in beliefs about winning was also identified by Amelia:
My belief about winning has definitely changed.

Um, winning was always kind of high pressure in terms of you need to get to the final placing to get to the next competition or to keep a contract, always fighting to qualify or fighting to be seen as the winners . . .
So I guess it moved . . .
It [became] more how far can I go in terms of international racing?
How fast can I go?
Like what is my physical limit?
And it shifted your outlook, and I guess your expectation shifts with that.

Similarly, Steve explained how his belief about winning changed over time as a result of experience: Yeah, it used to be sort of the, yeah, want to win at all cost, but now it's as I've got a bit older, and experienced [how I view] winning has changed.
It's setting out to develop and achieve different things throughout the game . . .
I think, yeah, the development is winning.
Hence, it appeared that when athletes' beliefs about winning changed, so too did the goals and expectations associated with winning.
Athletes' beliefs about winning were reflected in differences in the goals they pursued, the outcomes they expected, and the attributions they made.
In this section, we detail the key contrasts between those who expressed proving and improving beliefs.
Those who communicated proving-oriented beliefs described goals directed towards proving dominance and continuing to win.
Several athletes noted that the goal of proving dominance was pursued even when superiority over competitors was apparent.

Harrison explained: 'There'd be times where you go to races and that you're overly dominant, and you still, instead of just taking it easy, you still go and win, to obliterate the competition . . . nothing less than complete domination was acceptable.'
Harrison's quote suggests that the goal was not simply to perform well enough to win, but to emphasise his dominance over the competition.
For others, the goal was not simply to win, but to continue winning.
Liam explained: 'When you're winning, you're at the top . . . the goal is to keep winning.
I wouldn't care how it affected anyone else, or how I did it, or anything.'
Hence, winning once was insufficient; being at the top created a position that subsequently had to be defended.
In addition, athletes who reported proving-oriented beliefs described pursuing goals relating to meeting others' expectations.
When asked about her goals, Lucy said:
I'd say I would probably-this is awful-but I probably would care more about having a really shit race and what people would think about that than potentially winning.
You know, when you're representing your country, you want to do that proud . . . we also had it from the coach, you know, saying, well, if you don't perform or you don't win, then that's you.
You're not at the next competition, and you could not get your funding for the next year.
Goals therefore included not only winning, but also meeting the expectations of others and avoiding the consequences associated with failing to meet them.
In contrast, those who expressed improving-oriented beliefs described goals focused on growth and meeting their own expectations.
As Amelia explained:
My goal, for sure.
I think [is that] I'm always trying to grow, to better myself in terms of what could I improve on to then make me go better.
I never really celebrated my wins at the time, more focused on what I could improve on if I'm honest.

Sophia described how, later in her career, she developed different goals for winning when playing in a less successful team and, in turn, appeared to adopt a wider definition of winning: I was playing for a [sports] team [later in career] that wasn't that successful.
So, as I say, I didn't get to experience a lot of winning, but I had my own intrinsic goals, and I was still winning in other ways . . . you sort of try and have not performancerelated goals.

In speaking about expectations, athletes commonly discussed expectations extending beyond anticipated sporting outcomes to include how they expected to think, evaluate their performance, and feel in relation to winning and losing.
Those who communicated proving-oriented beliefs expected to evaluate their performance through comparison with others.
Harrison explained: You have to feel like you're always fighting someone.
I used to compare myself to [name of rival] a lot, in training, in the performance . . . he wanted to win badly, I want to win badly.
So it's kind of you constantly compare.
Performance was therefore expected to be evaluated relative to other athletes.

On the other hand, those who expressed improving-oriented beliefs expected to evaluate performance against their own standards and to experience satisfaction with performance even without placing first or securing a podium finish.
For example, Chloe explained:
My expectation going in is I just want to live up to my own standards and being my best . . .

I think just if we, like, go out and have a race that we have executed really well, and performed how we knew we were capable of performing, I think is probably the most gratifying thing that I would experience.
Then if you win with that, it's really special.

Satisfaction was therefore not contingent on coming first or obtaining a podium finish; athletes could experience gratification from meeting their own standards and performing to their perceived capabilities, with outcomes of this kind representing an additional rather than necessary condition for satisfaction.
Those who expressed proving-oriented beliefs, by contrast, expected satisfaction with performance to be contingent on winning.
For example, Liam said: Yeah, I think there's that you start winning.
There's the expectation that you're going to keep winning from yourself, and from sponsors and coaches and stuff.
So that, and then when you do [win] you're gonna be happy, when you don't, yeah, it can be upsetting for everyone.
Furthermore, losing was expected to decrease motivation.

Lucy explained that failing to win could lead to reduced motivation and questioning the purpose of continuing: I kind of really struggle when I've lost or not medalled, and find myself in quite a kind of a dark hole kind of thing [and] question why I'm doing it . . . after each loss it gets harder and harder I'll lose motivation and start thinking, what's the point and [I] have considered quitting a number of times.

text.text: Those who expressed improving-oriented beliefs also expected losing to have positive psychological effects.
For example, Sophia emphasised:

Because there are all these things that people talk about that losing will give you, you know, resilience, the ability to keep going when the going is tough, and, you know, being motivated by things other than winning, like all of that sort of stuff.
So, like, I definitely expected all of that.
All athletes expected to take lessons from losing.

Zoe described how losing makes one a better athlete: Similarly, Harrison also felt that learning was an expectation even when the goal was to prove dominance: 'Every single race, irrespective of if you do win or lose, there's always a quite big diagnostic process . . . you can't keep winning if you don't keep learning how to be the best.'
Learning from losing therefore did not distinguish proving-oriented from improving-oriented beliefs.

Rather, the difference lay in the purpose that learning served: in improving-oriented accounts, learning was valued as part of development itself, whereas in proving-oriented accounts, it could serve the continued pursuit of preeminence.
Athletes who reported proving-oriented beliefs attributed losing to weakness and not being good enough.
Liam explained, 'If I lost, I'd think it was a weakness, either mentally or physically'.
Likewise, Isabella stated that 'You're basically not as good as them . . . sometimes you're just not good enough'.
In this sense, losing was attributed to perceived capability, rather than to particular aspects of their performance that could be identified and addressed.
Attributions of losing also involved assigning blame to other people.
Lucy explained how losing could lead to blame being directed towards teammates or referees:
When you're losing, people are down, generally blaming your teammates, or perhaps blaming the referee for not winning, or the [position] for missing, or whatever.
Whereas when you win, you forget about all those things and you just remember the outcome.
Conversely, those who reported improving-oriented beliefs attributed losing to specific performance gaps that needed to be addressed.
For instance, when asked about her response to losing, Amelia said: 'I think it certainly shows your gaps or mistakes you've made.
That you've gotta take forward to the next race or in your training.
So I definitely think not winning has been helpful.'

Zoe described this process in greater detail: So there's lots of little gems that can come from a loss . . . it might just be one little micro skill or one little moment in the game that was the breakdown . . . and usually I don't sleep the night of a game, so I would rewatch the game again and then I'd clip stuff that I'm like, I can be better at that next time.
But lots of video analysis.
This was not an absence of recognition on the part of the athlete that she had lost.
Zoe still identified shortcomings in her performance; however, the attribution was Sophia highlighted the role of others: 'I wasn't winning on my own.
I was winning with 11 other teammates and coaches, physios, and so forth'.

These shared attributions indicate that preparation, effort, execution, and support were common across both sets of beliefs; what differed was the meaning of winning itself and the purpose these efforts served.

Taken together, the ways in which beliefs about winning were connected to athletes' goals, expectations, and attributions support our interpretation that these beliefs functioned as a mindset about winning (see Table 1 for a synthesis).

text.text: Within this mindset, two contrasting sets of beliefs were evident.
Winning-is-Proving (WIP) encompassed beliefs that winning meant beating others and not losing.

While the former emphasises dominating the competition and the latter maintaining one's position at the top, both beliefs about winning are more akin to victory, which, in this sense, can be defined as a decisive triumph over an enemy, rival, or competitor (HarperCollins, n.d.-a, n.d.-b).

Associated goals and expectations emphasised demonstrating dominance, continuing to win, meeting others' expectations, and evaluating satisfaction in relation to winning, while losing was attributed to weakness, not being good enough, or the actions of others and external forces.
In contrast, Winning-is-Improving (WII) encompassed beliefs that winning meant realising potential and self-betterment.

While the former emphasises expressing one's capabilities and the latter ongoing improvement, both beliefs about winning are more akin to accomplishment, which, in this sense, can be defined as something successfully achieved through repeated effort, focus, and dedication (Cambridge University Press, n.d.), without necessarily requiring an adversary (HarperCollins, n.d.b).

Associated goals and expectations emphasised development, personal standards, and satisfaction that was not contingent on winning a competition or placing in an event, while losing was attributed to identifiable gaps in performance that could subsequently be addressed.
Importantly, learning from loss was evident across both sets of beliefs, as were attributions of winning an event or competition to preparation, effort, execution, and the support of others.
These shared features suggest that, in themselves, learning from loss and explanations for winning did not distinguish WIP from WII.
Rather, the distinction lay in what athletes believed about winning itself and the goals, expectations, and attributions associated with those beliefs.

In this sense, beliefs about winning constituted a mindset, while together this mindset and its associated goals, expectations, and attributions formed the broader meaning system through which athletes experienced winning and losing.  winning rather than being confined to sport (Crum et al., 2013).

text.text: A particularly noteworthy finding was that several athletes recalled that their beliefs about winning had shifted over the course of their careers through experience, reflection, or the influence of others, with associated changes in their goals and expectations.

This finding is consistent with prior research suggesting that mindsets can change through exposure to new information, messages from influential others, or conscious choice (Gasteiger & Crum, 2025), lending further support to the interpretation that these beliefs about winning are indicative of a mindset.

text.text: Another noteworthy finding pertains to the goals athletes pursued.

Existing studies of athletes' goal orientations emphasise task and ego orientations, two main types of goals related to Achievement Goal Theory (AGT; Nicholls, 1984), which reflect how athletes judge whether they have demonstrated competence or feel successful in sport.

text.text: Task-oriented athletes feel successful when mastering challenges, whereas ego-oriented athletes feel successful when they perform better than others (Roberts et al., 1998).

text.text: Not surprisingly, given this conceptual proximity, WIP beliefs were more closely associated with ego goals, whereas WII beliefs were more closely associated with task goals.
However, our data indicate that mixed associations are also possible.

For example, an athlete may feel successful when overcoming challenges or mastering a skill (i.e., task orientation), while simultaneously believing that winning means defeating a rival and proving they are the best (Winning-is-Proving).
Consistent with this logic, at least one participant made explicit how training, execution, and effort served as a means to win: to beat the competition and prove they were the best.

One possible explanation for this mixed pattern is that winning mindset operates at a higher level of abstraction than achievement goal orientation, capturing broad, organising beliefs about the nature and meaning of winning (Yielder et al., 2026; Zion et al., 2025).

text.text: Accordingly, research is underway to develop a measure of winning mindset and to empirically test its relationship with task and ego goal orientations.
Although preliminary, our results may be valuable to coaches promoting task-involving motivational climates that encourage learning and continual improvement (Sarrazin et al., 2001).

text.text: Winning mindset may, for reasons described above, offer a complementary and potentially valuable framework for coaches and support staff to understand what winning itself means to the athlete and how that mindset may orient goals and behaviours.
Moreover, our findings advance mindset theory by providing evidence for a new mindset category: mindsets about winning.

Further, our findings add to the growing body of sport psychology literature demonstrating the importance of beliefs, mindsets, and other psychological factors in how elite athletes approach winning (Hoffmann et al., 2026; Ittlinger et al., 2025; Kreiner-Phillips & Orlick, 1993).
text.formatted: Further, our findings add to the growing body of sport psychology literature demonstrating the importance of beliefs, mindsets, and other psychological factors in how elite athletes approach winning <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hoffmann et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Ittlinger et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kreiner-Phillips & Orlick, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: More particularly, our results are the first to shed light on elite athletes' beliefs about the nature of winning in general and provide initial empirical support for the existence of a distinct winning mindset.
One key limitation of this research is that our sample was largely female and comprised nine elite athletes representing seven sports from New Zealand.
Thus, we are currently unable to establish the prevalence of WIP or WII or determine whether the same sets of beliefs occur across countries, competitive levels, sports, or other domains.
Future research is therefore needed to test the proposed winning mindset in larger and more diverse samples and determine whether other populations hold similar or different beliefs about winning.
Although conducive to addressing our research questions, it cannot establish temporal or causal relationships between an athlete's winning mindset and their responses to winning and losing.

It will therefore be important for future research to determine whether WIP and WII predict affective, motivational, attributional, and behavioural responses following actual wins and losses, while longitudinal work examining whether an athlete's winning mindset can change across seasons, career stages, and major sporting transitions is also warranted.

Notions of a 'winning mindset' abound in popular talks, self-help books, podcasts, and sport psychology publications, yet despite its widespread use, there is little to no compelling empirical data to support the existence of such a mindset.

We suggest that the present study provides the first preliminary evidence of a winning mindset among elite athletes and, in so doing, establishes the foundation for research currently underway to develop and validate winning mindset as a novel psychological construct.
